notes.meaning: Zechariah sees four chariots coming out from between two mountains made of bronze. Bronze mountains picture the firm, unshakeable purpose and dwelling of God. From His presence, God sends out His power to govern and judge the nations.

Each chariot is pulled by horses of a different color: red, black, white, and dappled. These teams are strong and ready to run their courses swiftly. They show the different ways God works among the nations, bringing times of war, distress, or victory.

Zechariah asks the angel speaking with him what these chariots mean. He sees something mysterious and humbly asks God's messenger for understanding. When we read God's word, we too should ask Him for wisdom to understand what He reveals.

The angel explains that the chariots are the four spirits or winds of heaven. They have been standing before the Lord of all the earth, waiting for His orders. Now they ride out as His swift servants to carry out His commands across the globe.

The chariot with black horses goes toward the land of the north, followed by the white horses, while the dappled horses head south. Babylon lay to the north of Israel, and Egypt lay to the south. God is sending His heavenly forces to deal with the world powers that had oppressed His people.

The strong horses are eager to go, but they do not move until the Lord commands them. When He gives the word to patrol the earth, they immediately set out across the land. Nothing in this world happens outside of God's timing and permission.

The Lord calls out to Zechariah with a message about the horses sent to the north. By bringing judgment on Babylon and rescuing His people, they have satisfied God's anger and brought rest to His Spirit. God keeps His promises to defend His people and deal justly with their oppressors.

The night visions come to an end, and a direct word from the Lord comes to Zechariah. God now tells the prophet to carry out a real-life prophetic action. This action points forward to the coming Savior and His glorious kingdom.

Zechariah is told to meet three men—Heldai, Tobijah, and Jedaiah—who had just arrived with gifts from Babylon. He must go that very day to the house of Josiah son of Zephaniah to receive their offerings of silver and gold. Even Jews living far away in exile wanted to give their wealth to help rebuild God's house in Jerusalem.

Zechariah is commanded to take the silver and gold and make a royal crown to place on Joshua the high priest. In Israel, kings came from David's family and priests came from Aaron's family, so a priest never wore a royal crown. Joshua is crowned here not for his own glory, but as a living picture of the coming Messiah.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars think the crown was originally intended for Zerubbabel, the royal descendant of David, but Joshua was named instead to avoid political suspicion under Persian rule.

notes.meaning: God announces a man named the Branch, who will sprout up from His place and build the temple of the Lord. The Branch is a prophetic name for the Messiah, the promised Savior from David's line. While Joshua helped rebuild the stone temple in Jerusalem, the true Branch builds the lasting spiritual temple of God's people.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Traditional Catholic translations render the title Branch as 'the Orient' or the rising dawn, identifying Christ as the divine dawn who restores the royal house of David.

notes.meaning: The Branch will be clothed in royal honor and sit on a throne to rule. He will also serve as a priest on His throne, joining the work of king and priest in perfect harmony. Because Jesus is both our King and our High Priest, His throne is a place of peace and mercy for all who trust Him.

differ.view: Some evangelicals teach that the Branch will build a literal temple in Jerusalem during a future thousand-year earthly reign, rather than ruling now from heaven over the church.

notes.meaning: After being placed on Joshua, the crown was to be kept inside the temple as a reminder. It honored the men who donated the gold and silver, and it confirmed that Joshua was not becoming an earthly king. Most of all, it stood in the temple as a visible pledge that the promised Priest-King would surely come.

People from far away will come and help build the temple of the Lord, showing that God truly sent His prophet. This pointed first to returning Jewish exiles and ultimately to Gentiles—people from all nations—being welcomed into God's spiritual family. The promise came with a call for God's people to listen to His voice and obey Him faithfully.
